text.content:
This is a complete evening of Don’t Get Forked for 3–5 players who have never played. It teaches the game as it goes: nobody needs to read the rulebook first, you included. Read this page and the next before your guests arrive; everything after that you can read aloud at the table.

How to Read This Script

  • Boxes marked “Read aloud” are for the players. Read them word for word.
  • Grey, smaller text is for you alone: what to ask, what to roll, what to write down.
  • The Places has a page for every place in town. When the party goes somewhere, turn to it.
  • When It Happens has a box for everything the dice can do: a Cost, Trouble, a chase, a capture, a Tell, the final flight. When it happens, turn to it and read.
  • The rules here are the rulebook’s, said in plain words. If you have the book, it agrees; if a question comes up that this script doesn’t answer, make a quick ruling and keep the night moving.

What You Need

  • Each player: one each of d4, d6, d8, d10 and d12, plus a second d6 (the Mask) and a second d10 (the Monster). Players can share if you’re short.
  • You: a d6 (for Tells and chases) and this script.
  • The Entity cards (The Eight Entities, near the end): one per Entity, with the rulebook’s defaults already picked. Print them and cut them out, so players can choose. The Castle Duty can be changed at the table (Part One).
  • The tracker (the last page): print it. It keeps Suspicion, the Turns, the Lead, the shopping list and the lock-up. A coin or a token on each track is enough.
  • The map of Hallowby (Hallowby at a Glance), on the table where everyone can see it. Players move a token or a coin to show where their Entity is.

The Evening at a Glance

20–25 minPart One: The Castle. Who the players are, the shopping list, choosing Entities and Castle Duties, a practice roll.
75–100 minPart Two: Into Hallowby. The raid: twelve Turns of sneaking, rolling, and maybe running.
0–15 minThe final flight, if the town turns out with pitchforks.
5–10 minPart Three: How the Year Went. What came home, and the epilogue.

Take a short break after Part One if your group likes one: it’s the natural pause before the raid.

The Night in Numbers

Hallowby is an Easy town. Keep these to hand (they’re on the tracker too):

  • The shopping list: 4 items. One is essential: the cask of red wine.
  • Turns: 12, then dawn. Charges: 3 for each Entity.
  • Suspicion: starts at 0. The Limit is 11: when Suspicion reaches it, the whole town hunts the party (the final flight).
  • The way out: Difficulty 6. The lock-up: Difficulty 10.
  • A local chase: the Lead starts at 1, escape at 4, against a mob of 8 plus half the Suspicion (rounded down, at most 12).
  • The final flight: the Lead starts at 2, escape at 5, against a mob of 10.

Running a Turn

The raid is twelve Turns. Each Turn, run this loop. It is on the tracker too.

  1. Say the Turn: “Turn 3.” Move the Turn marker.
  2. Go round the table. Ask each player, “What does your Entity do?” Each takes one action: roll at the next obstacle where it is, move to another place, pick up dropped items, or wait. They act one at a time, in any order they like, and each result counts at once.
  3. A move takes the Turn: the Entity is there now. Turn to that place’s page and read its arrival box. If it’s a watched place that nobody has reached yet, make a Tell check once everyone moving there this Turn has arrived (When It Happens).
  4. A roll: ask which trait, Mask or Monster, and whether anyone spends a charge. Then they roll, you read the result, and you mark any Suspicion. One roll raises Suspicion once, by its biggest trigger.
  5. End of the Turn: if the mirror has been taken and is still in town, Suspicion +1. If that was Turn 12, dawn comes (When It Happens).

Whenever Suspicion reaches 11, stop wherever you are and turn to The Final Flight.

Keeping it moving

  • Let the players plan out loud, but if a Turn stalls, ask the quietest player first.
  • The party may split up. Hallowby is small enough to visit together, but splitting saves Turns.
  • When a player asks “can I…?”, the answer is usually “yes, if you get past the obstacle”. Every place is in this script; nothing else needs a roll.
  • Be generous with the funny voices and stingy with the rules talk: the script holds the rules, so you don’t have to.

Easy. A market town that takes Lantern Night very seriously, and real monsters not at all.

Lantern Night: Turnip lanterns in every window.

The shopping list (4 items):

  1. A cask of red wine (“for the guests”) (essential)
  2. A pot of nightshade (purely ornamental)
  3. Hinges that creak properly
  4. A new cape

The furniture: a gilt mirror (Bulky: one carrier), at the tailor (4).

Villagers: old Granny Mott, who has seen it all before (carrying a lantern and a pitchfork “for the parade”); a gang of children (judging the costume contest).

Easy: Suspicion Limit 11 · Difficulty: the way out 6, the lock-up 10 · the final flight: mob 10, Lead 2, escape at 5.

Reading the key. Each location’s rows run in order: its two ways in (the party picks one the first time anyone tries the location, then keeps it for the night), then each “Then”. Watched: Trouble there gets you caught. (group): each Entity rolls for itself. The loud way works too, at Suspicion +1 whatever the result. The guard dog’s Difficulty is already 2 harder: it guards the furniture. On the map, an eye marks a watched location and the star marks the mirror. Every move takes one Turn (two carrying the mirror).

About 20–25 minutes. Have the Entity cards face up in the middle of the table, the map of Hallowby where everyone can see it, and the tracker beside you: Suspicion 0, Turn 1. When everyone is settled, begin.

Welcome

Tonight’s Halloween, so tonight we play monsters. Not people dressed up as monsters: real ones. The kind who have to dress up as people dressing up as monsters.

You all live together in a castle in the woods above a town called Hallowby. The castle is draughty, it creaks in all the wrong places, and the larder is empty.

Once a year, the town has its festival: Lantern Night. Everyone in Hallowby puts on a costume, lights a lantern and walks the streets till dawn. It is the one night of the year a real monster can stroll down the high street and get complimented on the outfit.

So once a year, you go shopping. You don’t pay.

You have until dawn to steal everything on the castle’s shopping list and get it home. If it goes well, Hallowby wakes up a few things short and blames the children. If it goes badly, the whole town turns out with pitchforks, and you run. If they corner you, you get forked. That’s the game: Don’t Get Forked.

The Shopping List

Point to the four places on the map as you read each item.

The list is pinned to the kitchen door, in spidery handwriting:

  • A cask of red wine, “for the guests”. It’s underlined three times. This one is essential: without it the castle can’t have a good year. It’s in the cellar of the tavern.
  • A pot of nightshade, purely ornamental. From the florist.
  • Hinges that creak properly. The new ones are far too quiet. From the carpenter.
  • A new cape. From the tailor.

And at the bottom, in different handwriting: “Also, a mirror would be nice.”

Bring home the wine, and miss no more than one of the other three, and it’s a good year: a Win. Do all that and bring home a piece of furniture too, and it’s a Grand Year. There’s a fine gilt mirror at the tailor’s.

Choosing Your Monster

Read the eight introductions, pointing to each card. Then let the players choose.

Eight monsters live in the castle. Each of you plays one, and no two of you play the same one.

  • Dracula, the smoothest talker in the castle. He can look a guard in the eye and walk straight past. Garlic is a problem.
  • Frankenstein’s Creature, the strongest. It breaks what others pick, and it can carry furniture like nobody else.
  • The Mummy, the cleverest. Three thousand years old, and it remembers every trick. Mind the loose threads.
  • The Werewolf, the fastest. If the wolf shows, the crowd just sees a very large dog.
  • The Invisible Man, the sneakiest. Nobody can catch what they can’t see, unless he’s carrying something.
  • A Ghost, who drifts through walls and slips past crowds. Cold iron is its trouble.
  • A Witch, the best friend to have at your elbow: her spell makes anyone’s roll better. Her black cat warns her of watching eyes.
  • Jekyll & Hyde, two monsters in one coat: a charming doctor, and a brute who comes out when he shouldn’t.

Pick one each and take its card.

Once everyone has a card, ask each player in turn to say their Entity’s name, so the table knows who’s who.

Your Card

Look at your card. Every monster has five traits: Brawn for force and lifting, Nimble for climbing and running, Sly for sneaking and stealing, Charm for talking and passing as human, and Wits for noticing and working things out.

Each trait is a die. You all have the same five, a d4, d6, d8, d10 and d12, in a different order. Your d12 is what you’re best at. Your d4, you’d rather not.

Every time you roll, you add a second die. You choose which. The Mask is a d6: you keep your costume on and pass as human. The Monster is a d10: you let the monster out. The Monster is stronger, but if its number comes up higher than your trait die’s, the town sees what you really are. That raises Suspicion, the whole town’s alarm, by 2.

Suspicion is one track for all of you. When it reaches 11, the whole town comes after you. So keep it low.

A Practice Roll

Nothing in this practice counts: no Suspicion, no charges. Ask each player to roll their d12 trait with the Mask d6, add them, and tell you the total. Read the box, then tell each player their result.

Every roll is against a number called the Difficulty: 6 is easy, 8 is normal, 10 is hard, 12 is very hard. Let’s say 8.

  • 8 or more is a Success. You do it.
  • 1 or 2 short, a 6 or a 7, is a Cost. You still do it, but something goes wrong, and I pick what.
  • 3 or more short is Trouble. You don’t do it, and Suspicion goes up. If someone was watching, you’re caught and you have to run.
  • And if both dice show the same number on a Success, that’s a Critical: something extra good.

Now roll the d12 again, this time with the Monster d10 instead of the Mask. Did the d10 come up higher than the d12? Then the Monster showed. It usually helps you succeed, but tonight, every time it shows, Suspicion goes up by 2. The Mask never shows.

Let them laugh at whoever’s Monster showed. Then go on.

Your Powers

Each of you has 3 charges. One charge pays for one use of an ability: your Signature or your Gift, both on your card. Spend it before you roll. Nothing passes on its own: you still roll.

Every ability does one of four things. It makes your trait die one size bigger. Or it lets you roll a different trait. Or it lets you roll the Monster without it showing. Or it opens a way past an obstacle that only you can take. Your card says which.

You can spend a charge on a friend’s roll too, if you’re in the same place. It costs your charge, not your action. Only one thing can make a die bigger on any one roll, though.

Run out of charges and you can still use an ability: that’s an overdraw, and it costs Suspicion +2 instead.

Your Perk is always on and free. Your Weakness is what the mob brings when it’s chasing you. Your Tell is the little thing that gives you away. Tonight, keep the Gift and Perk your card shows.

Castle Duties

Last thing. Everyone at the castle has a job, a Castle Duty, and does the shopping for it. At the place where your Duty’s item is, your trait die is one size bigger on your own rolls there.

Tonight’s list needs a Cook for the wine, a Gardener for the nightshade, a Handyman for the hinges and a Tailor for the cape. The Butler and the Librarian have nothing to buy tonight.

Your card has a Duty already. Keep it, or swap to any Duty nobody else has. No two of you can have the same one.

If two players want the same Duty, the one who chose their Entity later picks another. Write each player’s Duty on the tracker. The six Duties are Cook, Gardener, Librarian, Butler, Handyman and Tailor.

Setting Off

The castle door groans open. Down the hill, between the trees, Hallowby glows: a turnip lantern in every window, music in the square, and somewhere a bell ringing for no reason at all.

You straighten your costumes. Well. Your costumes.

Let’s go shopping.

Turn to Part Two.

About 75–100 minutes, the final flight included. Read the next two boxes, then start Turn 1.

The Edge of Town

The path comes out of the woods at the bottom of the hill, by a little humpbacked bridge. That bridge is your way out: when it’s time to go home, you all meet back here.

Across it, Hallowby is in full swing. Turnip lanterns grin from every window. A fiddle band is murdering a jig in the square. Children dressed as bats chase children dressed as ghosts. An old woman with a lantern and a pitchfork, “for the parade”, gives you a long look, and decides you’re in costume.

You’re in.

How the Night Works

The night lasts 12 Turns. When the twelfth is over, the sun comes up.

Each Turn, each of you does one thing: roll to get past something, move to another place, pick up something that was dropped, or wait. You go one at a time, in any order you like, and everything happens straight away. You can split up.

Moving anywhere on the map takes one Turn. There are the four places on the list, the lock-up, and the bridge.

Every place has obstacles: a locked door, a guard dog, a nosy shopkeeper. You get past them in order, and whoever gets past the last one has the item. Each obstacle tells you which traits work and how hard it is.

Every place has two ways in. The first time any of you tries a place, you choose one, and that’s your way in there for the rest of the night.

Once one of you gets past an obstacle, it stays beaten for everybody. The exception is a crowd: everyone gets past a crowd for themselves.

Some obstacles have a loud way. It works, but it puts Suspicion up by 1, whatever you roll.

Some obstacles are watched. Get Trouble at a watched one, and you’re caught: you run for it. If the crowd corners you, you go in the lock-up, and the others can get you out.

You can hand things to each other any time you’re in the same place, and you can carry as much as you like. Except the mirror: that’s furniture, and furniture is heavy.

When you’re done, everyone who isn’t locked up meets at the bridge, and one of you rolls to get you all out of town.

And remember Suspicion. If it reaches 11, or you’re still in town when the sun comes up, the whole town hunts you, and you run for the castle together. That’s the final flight. That’s how monsters get forked.

Then begin.

It’s Turn 1. Where do you go?

If they can’t decide: the tavern cellar is a gentle first stop, since nothing there is watched, and it has the essential. Turn to The Places for wherever they go.

Your first roll: walk them through it

  1. The first time anyone tries a place: “Which way in?” Read both, then they choose.
  2. “Which trait?” Only a trait the obstacle lists, unless an ability says otherwise. Read them the choices.
  3. “Mask or Monster?”
  4. “Is anyone spending a charge?” Before the roll: theirs, or a friend’s at the same place.
  5. Castle Duty: if this place has the item for the roller’s Duty, their trait die is one size bigger (a d8 becomes a d10; a d12 stays a d12). That’s the roll’s one bigger die: no ability can add another.
  6. Roll and add, and compare with the Difficulty: a Success, a Cost (1–2 short) or Trouble (3 or more short). Doubles on a Success: a Critical.
  7. Suspicion: the loud way +1, Trouble +1, the Monster shows +2. One roll raises it once, by its biggest: the loud way and the Monster showing make +2, not +3.
  8. Read the result’s line from the obstacle. A Cost or Trouble: turn to When It Happens.

What Raises Suspicion

Trouble+1
The Monster shows+2
Taking the loud way+1, whatever the result
A Cost picked as Suspicion+1
Overdraw+2
A Tell goes off+1 (not from a roll)
The mirror, once taken+1 at the end of every Turn, even set down, until it leaves town, is lost or is abandoned

One roll raises Suspicion only once, by its biggest trigger, overdraw included. Good results never lower it. It never goes past 11: when it reaches 11, the final flight starts at once.

One page for each place on the map. When anyone arrives, read the arrival box. The first time anyone tries a location, read both ways in and let them choose; they keep that way in for the night. Each obstacle has its own box: read it, read the roll line, then read the line for the result. A Cost, Trouble or anything else the dice do: When It Happens.

The cask of red wine (essential) · food and drink: the Cook’s trait die is one size bigger here · nothing here is watched, so no Tell check and nobody gets caught here.

The Grinning Turnip is the loudest building in Hallowby tonight: fiddles, singing, and a queue out of the door. Nobody is looking round the back.

Behind the tavern, a muddy yard full of geese leads to the kitchen door. In the alley beside it, a heavy trapdoor drops to the cellar. Which way?

Way in · The goose yard

The yard is ankle-deep in mud and full of geese. Geese are the worst guards in the world, or the best, depending which side of them you’re on.

Sly to tiptoe through. Or Nimble, the loud way: run for it, honking. Difficulty 6. Not watched.

Success: Not one honk. The kitchen door is on the latch, and the cellar steps are right inside.

Trouble: One goose sees you. Then all of them do. You back out of the yard, covered in mud, to a chorus of honking. (Suspicion +1. Nobody is watching: no chase.)

or Way in · The cellar trapdoor

In the alley, an oak trapdoor, iron-bound and as heavy as a coffin lid.

Brawn. Difficulty 8. Not watched.

Success: It lifts with a groan nobody hears over the fiddles. Steps lead down into the dark.

Trouble: It won’t budge, and something in your back goes ping. (Suspicion +1. No chase.)

Then · The back room

The cellar is one dark, cluttered back room: barrels, sacks, a broken mangle, forty years of things nobody threw away. The wine is in here somewhere.

Wits to work out which barrel. Or Sly, the loud way: rummage through everything. Difficulty 8. Not watched.

Success: There, behind the pickled onions: a small cask, its label in faded red. For the guests.

Trouble: You bring down a shelf of saucepans. Upstairs, the fiddles stop. A long pause. Then they start again. (Suspicion +1. No chase.)

Whoever got past the back room is holding the cask of red wine. The essential is yours.

Mark the wine on the tracker, with who carries it.

The pot of nightshade · plants and seeds: the Gardener’s trait die is one size bigger here · watched: the first time anyone arrives, make a Tell check once everyone moving here this Turn has arrived (When It Happens).

Thorne’s the florist is selling festival garlands as fast as Mrs Thorne can wrap them. The shop floor is packed with people in costume, and Mrs Thorne, behind the till, sees every one of them.

The nightshade sits on a high shelf at the back. Up the side wall, a rickety drainpipe runs to an open window just above that shelf. Which way?

Way in · The crowded shop floor group · watched

Wall-to-wall witches, skeletons and one very hot man in a bear suit, all queuing for garlands.

Sly to slip through the crowd. Difficulty 8. Watched. It’s a crowd: each of you who wants past rolls for yourself. Whoever gets through takes the pot; if several get through at once, you choose who.

Success: A bit of elbow, a lot of “pardon me”, and the nightshade is in your hands.

Trouble: Someone treads on your foot. You yelp, in a voice that isn’t quite human, and the whole shop turns round. “Thief!” (Suspicion +1, and caught: a local chase.)

If two or more roll the crowd in the same Turn, that’s a group check: When It Happens. A Ghost with its Spectral Perk isn’t stopped by a crowd: it walks through with no roll, unless it’s carrying something.

or Way in · The drainpipe

The alley beside the shop is empty. The drainpipe is held to the wall with three rusty brackets and a prayer.

Nimble to climb it. Difficulty 10. Not watched.

Success: Up, in through the window, and the nightshade is right there on the shelf.

Trouble: The drainpipe comes away from the wall, with you on it. You land in a water butt. (Suspicion +1. No chase.)

Whoever got through has the pot of nightshade. Purely ornamental.

Hinges that creak properly · tools and hardware: the Handyman’s trait die is one size bigger here · watched: Tell check on the first arrival.

The carpenter’s workshop is shut for the festival. The lane outside is busy with families heading for the square, and every few minutes the night watchman’s lantern comes bobbing past on his round.

The front door is locked. Round the back, a high garden wall hides the timber yard. Through the window you can see the hinges, hanging on a board above the workbench. Which way?

Way in · The front door watched

A stout front door with a good lock, in full view of the lane.

Sly to pick the lock. Or Brawn, the loud way: kick it in. Difficulty 8. Watched.

Success: Click. The door swings open on hinges that, tragically, don’t creak at all.

Trouble: The pick snaps in the lock, and a man dressed as a pumpkin asks what you think you’re doing. (Suspicion +1, and caught: a local chase.)

or Way in · The garden wall

A high brick wall with broken glass along the top, and a padlocked gate.

Nimble to climb it. Or Brawn, the loud way: through the gate, lock and all. Difficulty 8. Not watched.

Success: Over the wall and down among the timber stacks. The back door isn’t even locked.

Trouble: Halfway up, the top of the wall comes away in your hands. (Suspicion +1. No chase.)

Then · The night watchman watched

You’re inside, but the workbench is right under the front window, and here comes the watchman’s lantern again.

Wits to time his round. Difficulty 8. Watched.

Success: Lantern left. Lantern right. Now. By the time he looks in, the board is empty and so is the room.

Trouble: He comes back early. The lantern swings round to you. “Oi!” (Suspicion +1, and caught: a local chase.)

Whoever got past the watchman has the hinges. They creak beautifully.

A new cape · cloth and costumes: the Tailor’s trait die is one size bigger here, the guard dog included · watched: Tell check on the first arrival · the mirror is here.

The tailor’s shop is lit up like a stage. Mrs Pinch, the tailor, stands behind her counter with a mouthful of pins, ready for last-minute repairs; the costume contest judges, a gang of very serious children, are due any minute.

The new cape hangs on a stand behind her. The side window is shuttered. And at the back of the shop, beside a tall gilt mirror, an enormous dog is asleep. For now. Which way?

Way in · Mrs Pinch at the counter watched

Mrs Pinch looks you up and down, and takes the pins out of her mouth.

Charm to talk her round. Or Sly, the loud way: snatch it from under her nose. Difficulty 8. Watched.

Success: You need it for the costume contest, you explain. She is so pleased someone appreciates a good cape that she wraps it for you.

Trouble: She peers at you over her spectacles. “That’s not a costume, dear,” she says. “That’s a face.” (Suspicion +1, and caught: a local chase.)

or Way in · The shuttered window

A side window in a dark passage, its shutters latched on the inside.

Nimble to slip the catch and climb in. Or Brawn, the loud way: force the shutters. Difficulty 10. Not watched.

Success: The catch lifts with a fingernail. In, out, and the cape is over your arm.

Trouble: The shutter swings back and bangs like a gunshot. Mrs Pinch drops her pins. (Suspicion +1. No chase: nobody saw who.)

Whoever got in has the new cape.

The Mirror

Once the cape has been taken, anyone past the tailor’s way in may try for the mirror. Taking it, once they’re past the dog, is free.

Then · The guard dog watched · for the mirror

The dog is the size of a small pony, and it’s lying across the mirror’s feet. One eye opens.

Charm: a biscuit and a pat. Or Nimble, the loud way: outrun it, barking. Difficulty 10 (it’s guarding the furniture). Watched.

Success: The dog thumps its tail twice, rolls over, and lets you have the mirror.

Trouble: The dog wakes up all at once, and all of it barks. (Suspicion +1, and caught: a local chase.)

The mirror is Bulky: one of you can carry it. While you do, you can’t use the Mask, your Nimble is one size smaller, and every move takes two Turns: after the first you’re somewhere in between.

And a mirror that size gets noticed. From now on, Suspicion goes up by 1 at the end of every Turn until it’s out of town. You can put it down any time, except while you’re being chased, but only giving it up for good stops the noise.

If Dracula is in the shop, the mirror shows the counter, the dog, the biscuit, and everybody except him (flavour only). Taking the mirror back up after it’s set down is an action. Abandoned, it stays where it is, makes no more noise, and can’t be taken again.

Always watched. The first time anyone arrives who isn’t a captive, make a Tell check. A captive’s arrival doesn’t count. Rescue and slipping free: When It Happens.

The lock-up is a squat stone hut behind the square, with one barred door, one barred window, and a constable asleep in a chair outside with his hat over his eyes.

Always watched. The first time anyone comes back here, make a Tell check. Only when everyone who isn’t locked up is here may one of them roll.

The humpbacked bridge at the edge of town. Families are crossing it with lanterns, heading home; beyond it the path climbs into the woods and up to the castle.

The way out watched

One of you rolls for everybody. Sly to slip across with the crowd, or Nimble to go along under the bridge. Or Brawn, the loud way: barge straight through. Difficulty 6. Watched.

Success or Cost: You’re across, and the woods close behind you. The Cost here costs nothing. Turn to Part Three.

Trouble: A dad with a lantern lifts it high, right into your face, and screams. (Suspicion +1, and the roller is caught: a local chase. Everyone can try again next Turn.)

Anyone still in the lock-up when you cross is left behind. Are you sure you’re all here?

A Cost

The roller does it, but you pick one cost. Never pick one that costs nothing right then: not Suspicion +1 on a roll that already raised Suspicion, not “drop an item” from someone carrying nothing, not a lost Turn when nothing is waiting. Check the roller’s Perk: the Mummy never loses a Turn as its Cost.

Read the line aloud
Suspicion +1You do it, but somebody noticed something odd about you. Suspicion goes up by 1.
Drop an itemYou do it, but in the scramble you drop something. It’s lying right here.
Lose a TurnYou do it, but it takes forever. You miss your next go.
Smaller dieYou do it, but you’ve twisted something. Your next roll’s trait die is one size smaller.

Drop an item: one item of loot the roller carries, which you pick: never what this roll wins, never the mirror. It stays in this place, and picking up dropped items is an action. Mix the Costs up; a dropped item is the most fun, because someone has to come back for it.

Trouble

It doesn’t happen, and Suspicion +1. Read the obstacle’s Trouble line. If the obstacle is watched, the roller is caught: turn to Caught. If not, that’s all: they can try again next Turn.

The Monster Shows

The Monster d10 rolled higher than the trait die: Suspicion +2, whatever the result. Not on a tie, and never with the Mask. If an ability let them roll the Monster without risking Suspicion (the Werewolf’s Good Dog, the Invisible Man’s Unseen, some Gifts), its showing adds nothing. Some Perks change this: Dracula’s Hypnotic Eyes, on Charm rolls. When the Monster shows on one of Jekyll’s rolls, the roll stands, and then Hyde takes over, free.

DraculaHis shadow stretches the wrong way across the street, and it has wings.
The CreatureIt straightens to its full height, and keeps on straightening.
The MummyA bandage comes loose, and keeps on unwinding, and there is nobody inside.
The WerewolfFur. A great deal of fur. And teeth.
The Invisible ManA glove waves cheerfully at someone, with nothing inside it.
A GhostIt flickers, and for a moment the wall behind it shows through.
A WitchGreen sparks crackle off her fingertips, and every lantern in the street flares.
Jekyll & HydeThe kindly doctor’s face twists into somebody else’s.

A Critical

A Success where both dice show the same number. Outside a chase, the roller gets back one charge it spent (never more than 3). In a chase, it counts as two Successes.

Perfect. Not a sound, not a witness. If you’ve spent a charge tonight, you get one back.

A Tell Check

The first time anyone reaches a watched place: the florist, the carpenter, the tailor, the lock-up (not a captive’s arrival) and the way out once anyone comes back to it. Each place is checked once a night. Wait until everyone moving there this Turn has arrived, then roll a d6. On 4–6, a Tell goes off: number the arrivals, roll to pick one, and read its line. Suspicion +1; that’s its only effect. The Witch’s Familiar’s Warning: if she is among the arrivals, a Tell goes off only if a second d6 also rolls 4–6.

Read the line aloud
DraculaA dark shop window reflects the whole street: the lanterns, the crowd, the grinning turnips. Everyone but you. Someone looks from the window, to you, and back.
The CreatureYou stand a head above the whole crowd, and no costume in the world hides it. A child on her father’s shoulders looks you right in the eye.
The MummyYou leave a trail of dust behind you, and a smell of old spices. A woman sniffs, frowns, and follows it with her eyes, all the way to you.
The WerewolfYour eyebrows meet in the middle, and there’s a little too much hair everywhere else. A man nudges his friend. “Good costume,” the friend says. “Very good.”
The Invisible ManBandages, goggles, a false nose, and then a sneeze, from nowhere at all. Three people say “Bless you” and look round for whoever sneezed.
A GhostThe candles gutter as you drift in, and everybody’s breath fogs. Someone pulls their shawl tighter and peers into the cold.
A WitchYour black cat sits down in the middle of the floor and stares at people. Unblinking. One by one, they stare back.
Jekyll & HydeOne of your hands is a gentleman’s. The other is hairy and knotted. Somebody shaking it notices.

A Group Check

When two or more roll the florist’s crowded shop floor in the same Turn. Everyone declares their trait, their die and any charges first, then all roll at once. Each gets past on its own result. Suspicion rises only once for the whole check, by the biggest single trigger among the rolls. Everyone who gets Trouble is caught together, and flees together on one Lead (Caught, below).

You go into the crowd together. Ready? Everybody roll at once.

Caught: the Local Chase

Trouble at a watched obstacle. The whole chase, however many rounds, happens inside this Turn. While it lasts, the runner can’t drop or hand over anything.

They’ve seen you. Somebody shouts. Somebody else grabs a broom. Run!

This is a chase. Your Lead starts at 1. Get it to 4 and you’ve lost them. If it drops to 0, they’ve cornered you.

Every round, I’ll tell you what the ground is like, and it gives you two traits to choose from. Roll one of them, with the Mask or the Monster, against the mob. A Success puts your Lead up by 1. Trouble puts it down by 1. A Cost leaves it where it is.

  1. The Lead starts at 1. The Werewolf’s Night Runner, fleeing alone: Lead 2.
  2. The mob’s Difficulty is 8 plus half the Suspicion, rounded down, at most 12. Work it out again at the start of every round. Suspicion 0–1: 8 · 2–3: 9 · 4–5: 10 · 6–7: 11 · 8–10: 12.
  3. Each round, roll a d6 on the ground table below and read the line. The runner picks one of its two traits, and the Mask or the Monster (no Mask carrying the mirror). Abilities go on the runner’s own roll only: nobody else can spend a charge on it. No Castle Duty in a chase, and no opening a way of your own.
  4. Move the Lead: a Success +1 (a Critical +2), a Cost no change, Trouble −1.
  5. Suspicion still rises in a local chase: Trouble +1, the Monster showing +2, an overdraw +2, once per roll, by its biggest trigger.
  6. The Weakness: from round 1 for Dracula and a Ghost, from round 3 for everyone else, the runner’s trait die is one size smaller to the end of the chase. Read its line when it starts.
  7. Escape at 4: they’re back where they were caught, with this Turn used up. Cornered at 0: captured (below).

Caught together (Trouble in the same group check): everyone in it rolls each round, in any order they like, and the Lead moves once for the round by the majority rule (The Final Flight). Suspicion rises once a round, by the biggest trigger. A Perk that changes a local chase only works for someone fleeing alone. If Suspicion reaches 11 during the chase, it ends at once and the runners join the final flight; anyone cornered that same round is captured first.

The Ground (d6, every round of any chase)

1The crowded squareLose yourself in the crowd, or bluff your way through. Sly, Charm.
2Back alleysDuck, dodge, double back. Nimble, Sly.
3The market stallsOverturn a cart, vault a stall. Brawn, Nimble.
4Over the rooftopsClimb, jump, find a way down. Nimble, Wits.
5The festival paradeJoin in: you’re in costume, after all. Charm, Sly.
6A dead endBreak through, or think fast. Brawn, Wits.

The Mob Brings Your Weakness

Read the line aloud
Dracula: GarlicRound 1Someone at the front is waving a string of garlic like a lantern.
The Creature: FireRound 3Somebody has lit the torches.
The Mummy: A Loose ThreadRound 3A small boy has hold of a loose end, and he is not letting go.
The Werewolf: HoundsRound 3Somebody has let the hunting dogs out.
The Invisible Man: FlourRound 3A bag of flour bursts all over you, and there you are.
A Ghost: Cold IronRound 1Horseshoes, railings, a poker from the fire: the street is full of cold iron.
A Witch: RowanRound 3Old Granny Mott has a sprig of rowan, and she’s holding it up at you.
Jekyll & Hyde: A Familiar FaceRound 3“Doctor Jekyll? Is that you?”

Captured

Cornered in a local chase. The town takes back everything the captive carried, the mirror included: it’s gone for the night, and nobody can take it again. Put the captive’s token in the lock-up.

Hands grab you from every side. Somebody sits on you. When you get your breath back, you’re in the lock-up, and the constable is very pleased with himself. Everything you were carrying is gone.

From next Turn, once a Turn, you can try to slip free. Or the others can come and get you. Anyone still in here when they leave town is left behind.

A captive can’t pick anything up or be handed anything, but can still spend charges on any roll at the lock-up: its own, a rescuer’s, or another captive’s.

Rescue and Slipping Free

A rescue watched

Anyone not held, at the lock-up (getting there is a move). Sly to sneak past the constable, or Brawn, the loud way: tear the door off. Difficulty 10. Watched.

Success or Cost: every captive there is free (pick a Cost as usual). The freed act again next Turn, from the lock-up.

The door swings open. The constable snores on.

Trouble: Suspicion +1, and the rescuer is caught: a local chase.

The constable’s hat falls off. He isn’t asleep after all.

Slipping free watched

The captive, once a Turn, from the Turn after its capture. Sly or Nimble, or Brawn, the loud way. Difficulty 10. Watched.

Success: free, and acts again next Turn, from the lock-up. A Cost: nothing happens. Trouble: Suspicion +1, but no chase.

The bars, it turns out, are only a suggestion.

The lock-up is watched, so Dracula’s Mesmerise works on both. A rescue frees only those held at that moment.

Dropping, Picking Up and Handing Over

An Entity may drop its own loot, or the mirror it carries, any time, free, except while it’s caught (until its chase ends). Dropped things stay in that place; dropped between places, they stay at the place it left, and an Entity that sets the mirror down there is back at that place too. Anyone there may pick up any number of dropped items, as their action for a Turn. Loot can be handed to anyone in the same place, free, any time: not while caught, and never to a captive.

Suspicion Rising

Flavour only. Read each line the first time Suspicion reaches that number, so the players feel the town waking up.

Read the line aloud
4Somewhere a dog starts barking, and doesn’t stop.
7The church bell starts ringing, though it isn’t the hour. In the square, someone says, quite loudly, “Those aren’t costumes.”
9Pitchforks are coming out of sheds. Nobody is saying “for the parade” any more.
10Lanterns are gathering in the square. One more thing, just one, and they’ll come for you.

Overdraw

At zero charges an Entity can still use an ability: it costs Suspicion +2 instead (part of that roll’s one rise). In the final flight it costs the Weakness instead (The Final Flight).

The End of a Turn, and Dawn

At the end of every Turn: if the mirror has been taken and is still in town (carried or set down, not lost or abandoned), Suspicion +1. Then move the Turn marker.

Read the line aloud
Start of Turn 10Over the woods, the sky is turning grey. The fiddles are slowing down.
Start of Turn 12This is the last Turn before dawn. The first birds are singing. Anyone still in town when the sun comes up will have to run for it.
End of Turn 12The sun comes up over Hallowby, and every costume in the street turns back into a person. Except yours.

After the end of Turn 12, everyone still in town who isn’t locked up: The Final Flight.

When Suspicion reaches 11, or dawn comes with anyone still in town. Stop wherever you are, even in the middle of a Turn or a chase. If a local chase was running, it ends at once and its runners join the flight; anyone cornered in that same round is captured first. Captives stay in the lock-up.

That’s it. Hallowby has had enough. The bells are ringing, the fiddles have stopped, and every lantern in town is turning your way: lanterns, pitchforks, rolling pins, the whole costume contest, and Old Granny Mott at the front.

Run for the castle. All of you, together, right now.

This is the final flight. Everyone who isn’t locked up runs together, wherever you were.

Your Lead starts at 2. Get it to 5 and you’re home. If it drops to 0, they’ve got you: you’re forked.

The masks are off now: everyone rolls the Monster, and Suspicion doesn’t matter any more. Every round I roll the ground, and it gives you two traits to choose from. Each of you rolls one of them against the mob, and you can spend charges on each other’s rolls.

Then we count. More Successes than Trouble, your Lead goes up by 1, or by 2 if you’re two or more ahead. More Trouble than Successes, it goes down the same way. Level, it stays. A Cost counts for neither, and a Critical counts as two Successes.

Anything you drop now stays in Hallowby.

Running It

  1. Who runs: every Entity who isn’t captured. The Lead starts at 2 (the Werewolf’s Fetch Perk: 3). Escape at 5. Cornered at 0: Forked.
  2. The mob’s Difficulty is 10, however many run. Suspicion has stopped: nothing raises it now.
  3. Each round: roll a d6 on the ground table (When It Happens) and read its line. Each runner picks one of its two traits. The Monster d10 only. Abilities may go on anyone’s roll. Everyone rolls, in any order the party likes.
  4. The majority rule: count the Successes (a Critical counts as two) and the Trouble; Costs count for neither. Successes ahead by 1: Lead +1; by 2 or more: +2. Trouble ahead by 1: Lead −1; by 2 or more: −2. Level: no change. Example: a Success, a Critical, a Cost and a Trouble make 3 Successes to 1 Trouble: Lead +2.
  5. The Weakness: the flight is a new chase for everyone, even someone who came straight from a local chase. From round 1 for Dracula and a Ghost, from round 3 for everyone else, the trait die is one size smaller to the end of the flight. Read its line.
  6. Overdraw now costs the Weakness instead of Suspicion: from the overdrawer’s own next roll to the end of the flight, its trait die is one size smaller. Once per flight each, and never while its Weakness is already in play. (So Dracula and a Ghost can’t overdraw in the flight.)

Home

The Lead reaches 5. Everyone in the flight is home, with everything they carry. Anyone still in the lock-up is left behind.

The last pitchfork falls behind in the woods. The castle door slams. Somewhere far below, Hallowby is still shouting at the trees.

You made it. Let’s see what you brought home.

Turn to Part Three.

Forked

The Lead reaches 0. The year’s result is Forked, whatever the party carries. Turn to Part Three and read only the Forked line.

They’ve cornered you at the bottom of the hill, with the castle’s windows glowing just above the trees. The lanterns close in. The pitchforks come up.

You got forked.

pages.name: Part Three: How the Year Went

text.content:
About 5–10 minutes. An item, or the mirror, is home if an Entity who got out of town carries it: by the way out, or by escaping the final flight. Find the result, then read its line.

Read the result’s line aloud
Grand YearA Win, and the mirror came home too.A year of plenty. The new piece goes in the great hall, and everyone pretends it was always there.
WinThe wine came home, and no more than one of the other three items is missing.Full larders, warm fires. The castle creaks happily through another year.
PartialNot a Win, but at least 2 of the 4 items came home. Without the wine, a Partial at best.The castle gets by, just. Someone has to sleep in the draughty tower.
Bust0 or 1 of the 4 items came home.A long, thin year, and a lot of arguing about whose fault it was.
ForkedCornered in the final flight, whatever came home.The town tells the story for years. Next Lantern Night, the bells ring a little louder.

Left behind: work out the result first, then drop it one step for each Entity left in the lock-up: a Grand Year becomes a Win, a Win a Partial, a Partial a Bust. It never drops below Bust.

Then, unless the result is Forked, read one line for each item that didn’t come home.

Read the line aloud
The wine (food and drink)Turnip soup every night until spring.
The nightshade (plants and seeds)Nothing grows but nettles, and the nettles win.
The hinges (tools and hardware)Every door in the castle creaks, sticks or falls off.
The cape (cloth and costumes)Next year’s disguises are held together with string and hope.

Goodnight

And that was Lantern Night in Hallowby. Somewhere down the hill, a town is counting its spoons, and a florist is wondering where the nightshade went.

Happy Halloween.

Want more? The rulebook has three more towns, and tables to roll your own.
